item.content:encoded:
Gov.-elect Tony Ada and Lt. Gov.-elect E.J. Calvo said their incoming administration will open cabinet and senior staff positions to public applicants, with an emphasis on professional experience, qualifications, and commitment to public service rather than political affiliation.

During their first press conference as governor and lieutenant governor-elect, the two outlined plans to establish an online application portal where interested residents, including current government employees, can submit resumes and apply for positions within the incoming administration.

Jadeen Perez, who will chair the transition team’s Committee on Administration and Appointees, said the committee plans to begin accepting applications after the election results are certified on Nov. 19.

Applicants will undergo background checks and an evaluation of their qualifications before the committee submits recommendations to Ada and Calvo.

Ada said the application process will be open to anyone interested in serving, including members of the current administration.

“The bottom line is, everybody working together, regardless of party affiliation,” Ada said. “Election is over. Now it’s time for everybody to come together and work together.”

The incoming administration has also established three principal transition committees to guide the transfer of government responsibilities. The Committee on Government Operations and Efficiency, chaired by Nate Denight, will review the operations of government agencies, identify opportunities to improve efficiency, and assess existing challenges. The Committee on Administration and Appointees will oversee the recruitment and evaluation of potential cabinet members and senior staff, while the Committee on Inaugural Arrangements, chaired by Piti Mayor Jesse Alig, will coordinate inauguration preparations.

Denight said the government operations committee will establish additional subcommittees to review the island’s 52 government agencies. The committees will meet with agency management and staff to identify what is working, what needs improvement, and what resources may be needed.

Their findings will be compiled into a final transition report outlining each department’s current situation, objectives, and recommendations. Transition chair Jerry Crisostomo said the report will help Ada and Calvo determine their administration’s priorities and guide appointments ahead of their expected Jan. 4 start in office.

Ada said the incoming administration will first focus on completing a smooth transition and assessing the government’s financial position and operational needs before determining its immediate priorities.

One policy direction the incoming administration has already identified is a dedicated executive leadership position for tourism and destination development, separate from economic development. Calvo said they may be the first administration ever to dedicate an executive position to the industry of tourism.

“The position we’re looking at is actually tourism and destination development, separate from economic development, which is important,” Calvo said, “I think that would probably have fallen under economic development in the past, but we need to look at diversifying our economy and also protecting other growing industries separately.”

Ada said the position would reflect tourism’s significant impact on Guam’s economy and employment, particularly as the island’s tourism industry continues to face challenges.

When asked about their first 100 days in office, Ada said the administration will begin implementing its campaign plans after evaluating the government’s needs and establishing its leadership team. Calvo identified tourism, economic development, federal relations, and education as among the areas that will require attention.

When asked what the new administration is most excited to begin working on as they work toward a smooth government transition, they said they plan to continue monthly community cleanups, which began during the campaign.

“We want to still get out there and keep our community clean,” Ada said. “We want to ensure that, as we continue to move along within the first 100 days of our administration, that we start implementing our plans and get it to what we said during our campaign. You’re going to start seeing the implementation of those plans come to fruition.”

Ada and Calvo said they will seek guidance from former Republican governors and lieutenant governors to assist with the transition. Those invited to serve as honorary transition advisers include former governors Felix Camacho and Eddie Calvo, along with former lieutenant governors Ray Tenorio, Mike Cruz and Kaleo Moylan.

The transition team says additional appointments and opportunities for public participation will be announced in the coming weeks. Updates are expected through the incoming administration’s website and social media platforms.

item.title: CNMI runoff elections set for Nov. 20 after certification
item.description: The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna. item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Election Commission is expected to certify the results of the 2026 general election Friday, formally triggering a 14-day countdown to runoff elections on Nov. 20 for governor and attorney general, according to CEC Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna.

Magofna said Thursday that election commissioners are scheduled to certify the official results, setting into motion preparations for the runoff election required under CNMI law when no candidate secures more than 50% of all votes cast and counted.

"So we have to have an election 14 days after," Magofna said.

The certification will finalize results from the Nov. 3 general election and establish the timeline for distributing runoff ballots and preparing polling sites across the Commonwealth.

According to the CEC, absentee voters who requested ballots for the general election will automatically receive absentee ballots for the runoff election. Election officials said no new requests for overseas absentee ballots will be accepted, although over-the-counter absentee voting will remain available.

Earlier, the commission mailed out 1,420 absentee ballots for the general election. Election officials counted 886 absentee ballots in the final tabulation and noted that ballots had to be received on Saipan on or before Election Day to be included in the certified results.

For the runoff election, the commission said it will continue to receive absentee ballots for up to 14 days after Election Day pursuant to its established procedures.

The certified results are expected to confirm runoff contests in both the governor's and attorney general's races.

In the gubernatorial contest, the Republican ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. led the field with 6,437 votes, or 49.5% of ballots cast, narrowly missing the majority needed to avoid a runoff. The independent ticket of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund Villagomez finished second with 5,043 votes, or 38.7%, advancing to the Nov. 20 runoff.

The independent team of Lawrence F. Camacho and Edith Deleon Guerrero placed third with 1,537 votes, or 11.8%.

The attorney general race also failed to produce a majority winner. Attorney Joaquin DLG Torres received 5,073 votes, or 39.7%, while attorney Michael Evangelista secured 3,854 votes, or 30.2%. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. followed closely with 3,836 votes, or 30.1%.

Under CNMI law, the top two vote-getters advance to a runoff when no gubernatorial candidate or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted.

The Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters for the 2026 election. More than 13,000 voters cast ballots in the gubernatorial race, leaving roughly 5,500 registered voters who did not participate.

Election officials said registered voters who did not vote in the general election remain eligible to cast ballots in the Nov. 20 runoff election.

With certification anticipated Friday, election administrators will have two weeks to complete preparations for what is expected to be a closely watched runoff that will determine the Commonwealth's next governor and attorney general.

item.description: The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body. item.content:encoded:
The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body.

A number of senators in the 38 th Guam Legislature gave up their seats to run for higher office. Republican Speaker Frank Blas Jr., Republican Vice Speaker Tony Ada and Democratic Sens. Therese Terlaje and Joe San Agustin all ran for governor, with Ada winning the island’s highest office.

Democratic Sens. Sabina Perez and Tina Muna Barnes ran for lieutenant governor.

That left nine incumbents, all of whom won reelection.

They are Republicans Sabrina Salas Matanane, Jesse Lujan, Chris Duenas, Shelly Calvo, Telo Taitague, Vincent Borja and Eulogio Shawn Gumatatao. Democratic incumbents reelected were Chris Barnett and William Parkinson.

Former Democratic Sens. Amanda Shelton, Telena Nelson and Clynton Ridgell were elected Tuesday, along with Democratic legislative newcomers Donna Quinata and Kallen Perez.

Hoa Nyugen is the Republican newcomer, giving the party an 8-7 majority in the 39 th Legislature.

item.title: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
item.description: Updated November 6, 2026 at 7:12 AM ChST ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 6, 2026 at 7:12 AM ChST

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.

Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.

Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.

As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.

Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.

"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."

The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.

Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.

Officials have appealed for calm. Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about $1,600 held by customers with no debts to Ueno. The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97% of clients.

On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud, alleging that Ueno made large loans to related companies without adequate guarantees and diverted some of the money to other group businesses.

Gustale's lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," José Fernández Zacur told local media.

Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Peña outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Peña's resignation did little to calm them. Many vowed to keep protesting until lawmakers finished impeaching him, saying his departure alone would neither bring accountability nor return their money.

"Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.

The Labor Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.

Many saw Ueno's collapse not just as reckless banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International's latest index of perceived corruption.

"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on Congress in the capital, Asunción, on Wednesday.

The crowds shouted, "We want your head, Peña!" Their signs branded him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded, "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets to push them back.

item.content:encoded:
The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.

Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.

"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."

"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.

During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.

The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.

Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.

"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."

Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.

Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.

The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.

In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.

"I'm proud of all we've accomplished during this time to ensure our nation's civil rights laws protect every American," she wrote in the email, a copy of which was obtained by NPR. "I'm also grateful for the hard work of the dedicated employees within the Division and the rest of the Department of Justice."

For many division veterans who were highly critical of Dhillon's treatment of career staff and her enforcement goals, her departure was a welcome development.

"Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."

"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

item.content:encoded:
We all have things we're tired of seeing on TV. For my part, I'd like to issue a 10-year moratorium on serial killers, self-destructive detectives, cute small towns that are rife with murder, and shows that open with an attention-grabbing chase or murder then follow with the words, "36 Hours Earlier," or "5 Weeks Ago" to alert us that the actual story is finally about to begin. I want no more Big Little Lies knockoffs or series that take 10 episodes to do what movies used to do in two hours.

I could go on, but I'd rather tell you why I love Small Prophets , the smash BBC hit now streaming on Apple TV. Composed of six elegant half-hour episodes, this gentle show is so original and consistently surprising that it's kind of a marvel. It blends deadpan humor, fantasy, social comedy and an alluring sense of melancholy to create a mood you'll love being inside.

Pearce Quigley plays Michael Sleep, a good-hearted, 50-ish man whose flowing locks and white beard make him look like a cross between an old hippie and Father Time. He lives in a suburban house, complete with an overgrown lawn, that he's kept the same since his partner, Clea, mysteriously disappeared seven years ago. Still hoping she'll return, he divides his time between half-hearted work at the Tool Box, a Home Depot-like store, and visits to the retirement home that looks after his inventive but scattered father, Brian — warmly played by Michael Palin .

His dad tells him about a friend in Egypt who was able to call up homunculi, miniature humanoid beings who can answer any question and always tell the truth. Brian gives his son the recipe for bringing these small prophets to life — they grow in glass jars — and suggests he ask them what happened with Clea. Although dubious, Michael decides to try, beginning a procedure that involves everything from old coins to a truckload of manure.

Meanwhile, other people start entering his life. He's shadowed by Clea's aggrieved brother Roy (played by Paul Kaye), who turns up broke and wants to claim the house. He becomes the obsession of his next-door neighbors — the comically hectoring Clive, who's tormented by Michael's messy yard, and his curious wife, Bev, who finds Michael interestingly different.

Above all, Michael develops an unlikely friendship with a disaffected young coworker Kacey, played by Lauren Patel. She bonds with Michael because he, too, has no time for their boss, Gordon — an officious incompetent with a greasy ponytail who's played by the show's brilliant writer-director, Mackenzie Crook. And all the while in Michael's shed, the homunculi are coming to life.

Small Prophets is the latest good show from Crook who specializes in series that tend to be tenderly offbeat, like his cult comedy Detectorists about members of a metal detecting club seeking buried gold. Believing that people are better than we might sometimes think, Crook casts a sympathetic eye on loners, oddballs, misfits and dreamers — many of them caught in unsatisfying jobs and thwarted hopes.

You feel his delicate touch in virtually all of Small Prophets ' characters, be it Michael, who yearns to recapture his vanished life with Clea, or Kacey, who does dead-end work but has huge, perhaps impossible dreams. Even characters who come off as foolish are drawn with loving care — they're vivid — and have moments where we glimpse something unexpectedly vulnerable hidden within them.

That said, Small Prophets is anything but doleful. Crook serves up some very good jokes — Michael's goofing on customers at the store is especially funny — and the show imbues daily life with poetic touches that feel magical, be it a falling star, an oil spill in the shape of a rabbit or a literally enchanting Christmas memory. When we finally meet the small prophets, they're haunting — fragile, truth-telling creatures whose faces bespeak pain and isolation. Trapped inside their bottles, they mirror the solitude of the human characters.

No one wears their inner wounds more appealingly than Michael, who carries us along with his strange charisma. Graced by Quigley's droll, confidently quiet performance, he embodies the positive approach that Small Prophets seems to believe in. Resolutely uncynical, Michael isn't merely caring and loyal and accepting of other people's differences. Without making a big deal of it, he leaves himself open to the wonder of life.
